#702. Latest Update: Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression

📅 14 Nov 2026

Latest Update: Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression

Tanggal: 14 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261113231624.htm

Industry observers note that A consistent daily routine may do more for your health than you realize. Researchers at the University of Missouri have found that older adults who follow regular daily schedules tend to experience less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggle to get a good night's sleep.

Recent findings suggest that the findings suggest that everyday habits, such as waking up, eating meals, socializing, and going to bed at consistent times, may play an important role in physical and mental well-being. By helping the body maintain its natural internal clock, a predictable routine could offer health benefits that extend beyond improved sleep.

In a recent development, the discovery could be especially important for older adults, who frequently experience sleep difficulties. According to the National Council on Aging, roughly half of adults age 60 and older report symptoms of insomnia, a condition that can make it difficult to fall asleep, stay asleep, or get restful sleep.

Daily Routines Linked to Less Pain and Depression.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate the relationship between sleep, daily habits, and overall health, Eunjin Tracy, an assistant professor in the College of Education and Human Development at the University of Missouri, examined survey responses from 67 older adults. Among the participants, 37 reported experiencing insomnia.

In a recent development, as researchers expected, those with insomnia generally reported more physical pain and higher levels of depression than participants without the condition. However, another pattern emerged when Tracy examined their daily routines.

Sources indicate that participants who maintained more consistent schedules tended to report less pain and fewer depressive symptoms, regardless of their sleep quality. This suggests that keeping regular daily habits may be associated with better health even when sleep problems persist.

"Regardless of sleep quality, those who reported having a regular daily routine had lower levels of physical pain and less depression compared to those without a daily routine," Tracy noted. "If we are consistent with when we wake up, eat, work or study, interact with others and go to bed, those time cues help synchronize our internal body clocks. Over the long term, that seems to be linked with improved health outcomes.".

One possible explanation involves the circadian rhythm, the body's natural 24-hour timing system. This internal clock helps coordinate when we feel awake or sleepy and influences numerous biological processes, including hormone activity, metabolism, and mood.

Rather than operating independently of our surroundings, the circadian system responds to signals that help it keep time. Light and darkness are especially important, but regular activities such as eating, working, interacting with others, and sleeping can also provide timing cues.

Industry observers note that when these signals follow a predictable pattern, they help keep the body's biological rhythms aligned. Irregular schedules, on the other hand, can interfere with that coordination.

"When we regulate our circadian rhythm well, our bodies function well, but if it gets too distracted, our bodies don't function as well," Tracy said.

Although the study did not establish that regular routines directly reduce pain or depression, the findings point to circadian regulation as one possible explanation for the connection.

Industry observers note that even relatively small changes in daily schedules may disrupt the body's internal clock. One common example is social jet lag, which occurs when a person's sleep schedule shifts between workdays and days off.

According to recent reports, someone who wakes up early throughout the week but stays up late and sleeps in on weekends may experience this mismatch. The resulting disruption resembles some of the effects of traveling across time zones, even though the person has never left home.

Tracy suggests that maintaining reasonably consistent schedules throughout the entire week, including weekends, may help limit these disruptions and support healthier circadian rhythms.

"As someone who wakes up and goes to bed at the same time every day, I think a daily routine can be helpful for people of all ages across their lifespan," Tracy remarked. "There is growing awareness about the concept of social jet lag -- waking up and going to bed at different times on weekends compared to weekdays -- and the disruptions it causes to our circadian rhythm, so hopefully this research helps more people consider the health benefits of a daily routine. Since one-third of our lives will be spent sleeping, I think health and well-being research should be looked at holistically from a 24-hour perspective and not just focus on when we are awake.".

A Simple Habit With Potential Health Benefits.

Industry observers note that the research highlights an aspect of healthy living that can be easy to overlook. While getting enough quality sleep remains important, the consistency of activities throughout the day may also be connected to how people feel physically and emotionally.

Recent findings suggest that because the study relied on survey data from a relatively small group of older adults, it cannot prove that adopting a regular routine will relieve pain or depression. Larger studies would be needed to establish whether changing daily schedules directly improves these outcomes.

Still, the findings suggest that a predictable daily routine may be a useful component of a broader approach to health, particularly for people experiencing insomnia.

For older adults and potentially people of other ages, simple habits such as maintaining regular waking times, eating meals on a consistent schedule, and limiting major changes in weekend sleep patterns may help support the body's natural rhythms.

The study, "Behavioral-social rhythms and insomnia symptoms: associations with pain, body mass index, and depressive symptoms among older adults," was published in the Journal of Behavioral Medicine.

#703. Diesel Prices Are Surging. This Electric Trucking Company Is Seeing More Interest

📅 14 Nov 2026

Diesel Prices Are Surging. This Electric Trucking Company Is Seeing More Interest

Tanggal: 14 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://insideevs.com/news/815472/diesel-prices-electric-trucks-einride/

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

High gas prices have helped drive more interest in electric cars this year. But it’s not just everyday drivers who are looking to ditch fossil fuels.

Eye-watering diesel costs are pushing more shippers to consider a switch to electric trucks, Roozbeh Charli, CEO of electric and autonomous freight tech giant Einride, told me in an interview.

“You’re definitely seeing an upswing in both customer conversations and just general narrative” around electrification, he noted.

Diesel prices have risen far more severely than prices for regular gasoline, putting extra pressure on commercial operators. The average cost of diesel in the U.S. has shot up by more than 60% since the war with Iran began, to over $6 per gallon. Shippers are facing far higher fuel costs in Europe too. It all means customers who told Einride they’d revisit the idea of electric freight sometime down the line are deciding to get the ball rolling.

“A lot of those customers are coming back now, saying ‘let’s get started, rather sooner than later,’” Charli said.

There’s some evidence that those conversations are generating actual business. Einride, which was founded in 2016 and sells electric freight services and software, says its sales pipeline tripled year over year during the first half of 2026. Its conversion rate doubled over the same period.

And it isn’t the only one noticing an uptick in demand. In September, a coalition of shippers like PepsiCo placed an order for 2,500 electric trucks in a deal that’s set to double the U.S. fleet of electric Class 8 trucks. Catalyst Mobility, one of the nonprofits running the program, has remarked it’s noticed more interest in EV trucks from companies that weren’t involved in the deal due to diesel prices.

Charli chalks the increased interest up to a couple of things. The pricing pain today is part of it. It means there’s a broader range of customer use cases where electric trucks are price-competitive with, or cheaper than, using traditional big-rigs. Those are typically what he calls “middle-mile” applications of, say, 100-200 miles back and forth, with high utilization. That last part is key, since battery-powered trucks still tend to cost more than diesel ones.

The situation is also making some companies realize just how exposed they are to drastic swings in the price of diesel, Charli noted.

Our weekly newsletter breaks down the biggest mobility news every Friday.

In a recent development, the trend is encouraging for reasons beyond economics. Heavy-duty trucks make up a relatively small portion of the U.S. fleet, but they account for a disproportionate share of fuel consumption and harmful air pollution.

“Any exposure to diesel exhaust is going to be harmful to your health,” says Ray Minjares, heavy-duty vehicles program director at the International Council on Clean Transportation. “And so since there's really no safe level, the obvious solution, particularly in a world where commercial zero-emission vehicles are already available, is to switch to that technology.”.

The Tesla Semi represents a "step-change" for electric trucking hardware in the U.S., Einride CEO Roozbeh Charli noted.

It has been revealed that high diesel prices aren’t the only tailwind helping to drive trucking electrification this year, Charli mentioned. The long-awaited launch of the Tesla Semi not only helped bring more attention to electric trucking, but it also introduced a genuinely groundbreaking offering to the U.S. market, he said.

“The Tesla Semi, in a U.S. context, is definitely a step-change in the capabilities of the hardware” in terms of range, performance, and price, he noted.

Industry observers note that in August, Einride announced aims to deploy 500 Semis to service Amazon and other North American customers, tripling its fleet. Tesla’s truck is several years late to full-scale production. But given the diesel situation these days, maybe it’s right on time.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

SpaceX plans to catch the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), and you can watch the action live.

Sources indicate that starship launched on its 15th test flight on Friday evening (Nov. 13), rising into the sky from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. The mission initiative called for bringing both of the vehicle's stages back to Starbase and catching them with the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — an unprecedented total recovery of an orbital rocket.

In a recent development, that didn't happen, however; SpaceX diverted Starship's Super Heavy booster to a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico 6.5 minutes after launch, for reasons that remain unclear. But a catch of the Ship upper stage is still on the table, and that would be historic in itself: SpaceX has never tried it before.

The Ship catch is scheduled to occur today at around 4:20 p.m. EST (2120 GMT; 3:20 p.m. local Texas time) — roughly 22.5 hours after Flight 15 lifted off. You can watch it live here at Space.com.

There's no guarantee that it will happen, however: If SpaceX detects anything off-nominal with Ship, it will scrap the catch attempt, as it did with Super Heavy on Friday afternoon. We'll just have to wait and see.

While the double-catch attempt was Flight 15's main headline, the mission had other objectives as well. One was getting Ship to orbit, which had happened on just one previous Starship launch — Flight 14, which lifted off on Sept. 28.

Ship deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 broadband satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO) on Flight 14, and it did so again on Flight 15. These 52 spacecraft are the first members of a constellation that will eventually consist of 100,000 satellites, if all goes according to SpaceX's strategy.

Sources indicate that and SpaceX aims to use Starship to build an even bigger network in LEO — Starmind, an AI data-center constellation that will harbor a million spacecraft, according to Elon Musk. (For context: SpaceX's current-gen Starlink network employs about 11,000 satellites at the moment.).

Assembling these megaconstellations will require an incredible launch cadence. And the double chopstick catch is key to that vision, SpaceX says, for it will enable quicker inspection, refurbishment and reflight of Starship.

So the company will doubtless try the maneuver again soon — probably on the next Starship flight, which won't be too far down the road.

#706. Latest Update: Yale scientists reveal what really slows aging and what doesn't

📅 14 Nov 2026

Latest Update: Yale scientists reveal what really slows aging and what doesn't

Tanggal: 14 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261112230452.htm

In a recent development, A growing body of research suggests that aging may be more flexible than once believed. Now, scientists at Yale have taken an crucial step toward identifying which treatments can actually influence biological aging and which ones show little measurable benefit.

Their findings suggest that certain prescription medications and lifestyle changes can reduce biological age as measured by DNA-based blood tests. Popular over-the-counter supplements examined in the research, however, showed little evidence of producing the same effects.

The findings, published in Nature Medicine, could help scientists evaluate anti-aging treatments more effectively, although researchers emphasize that changes in biological age markers do not necessarily mean people will live longer or avoid age-related diseases.

From Fighting Cancer to Understanding Aging.

It has been revealed that when Raghav Sehgal began graduate school at Yale several years ago, he planned to use advanced computer science techniques to investigate cancer. His background in engineering and experience launching a computational biology startup had given him a strong foundation for that work.

Industry observers note that however, a question from his Ph.D. adviser at the Yale School of Medicine changed his research direction. Rather than focusing on individual diseases such as cancer or cardiovascular disease, why not investigate the aging process that contributes to their development?

It has been revealed that "That put me on a different path," remarked Sehgal, now an associate research scientist in psychiatry who specializes in computational biology and bioinformatics. "As researchers, we have a long way to go in understanding the aging process and whether the steps we take to manage it really work.".

Sehgal now studies the biological mechanisms behind human aging, how scientists can measure those changes, and why getting older increases the likelihood of conditions such as cancer, diabetes, and dementia. His work also explores whether interventions might reverse certain aspects of biological aging, even if eliminating aging itself remains beyond reach.

Latest DNA Tests Reveal Which Anti-Aging Treatments Work.

Sehgal is the lead author of the latest study, which was conducted in the laboratory of Albert Higgins-Chen, an assistant professor of psychiatry at the Yale School of Medicine. The research team set out to determine which existing approaches to slowing aging produce changes that can be reliably measured.

According to recent reports, their analysis found encouraging results for certain medications and lifestyle interventions. In contrast, the over-the-counter supplements included in the study generally failed to produce meaningful reductions in biological age.

The project involved the entire Higgins-Chen laboratory, including Daniel Borrus, Jenel F. Armstrong, John Gonzalez, Jessica Kasamoto, and Yaroslav Markov.

It has been revealed that "For the first time we've shown that certain therapies have measurable impacts," mentioned Sehgal. "This wasn't previously possible, because we didn't have enough data to say these biomarkers are consistently responsive to these interventions.".

Biomarkers provide measurable information about what is happening inside the body. In aging research, they can help estimate a person's biological or functional age, which may differ from their chronological age.

To investigate whether treatments could influence aging, the Yale team relied primarily on blood-based measurements called epigenetic clocks.

It has been revealed that these tools analyze chemical patterns attached to DNA, particularly methyl groups (basic chemical structures that act like tags). Previous research has shown that these chemical markers change as people grow older. Some interventions may reverse certain age-associated patterns, and computer algorithms use those changes to estimate a person's biological age.

The researchers brought together findings from 51 clinical studies investigating different anti-aging strategies. These ranged from dietary supplements and medications to lifestyle changes and medical procedures.

In a recent development, across those studies, the team examined more than 110 DNA methylation biomarkers (including 16 major epigenetic clocks). By comparing measurements taken before and after interventions, they could evaluate which approaches were associated with reductions in biological age.

According to recent reports, "What we did was pretty unique," Sehgal stated. "We already know that certain things might prolong health span and lifespan. There is data from retrospective analysis as well as from animal models. We took all that knowledge along with the real-world clinical studies to identify which interventions in humans were slowing down aging across the board in these known biomarkers.".

Which Anti-Aging Treatments Showed the Best Results?

The researchers divided the interventions into four main groups: prescription drugs, lifestyle modifications, over-the-counter supplements, and medical procedures.

One of the clearest findings involved diet and exercise. Combining regular physical activity with a healthy eating strategy consistently reduced epigenetic age. The dietary approaches examined included Mediterranean, low-fat, and low-carb diets.

The strongest reductions in biological age markers were associated with certain pharmaceutical treatments. These included metformin and semaglutide, prescription medications used to manage metabolic conditions and body weight, as well as anti-TNF therapies that target a protein involved in the body's inflammatory response.

(TNF, or tumor necrosis factor, is an immune-system protein that helps fight inflammation-related injury.).

The findings were less encouraging for over-the-counter supplements and some medical procedures. In the studies examined, these approaches did not produce measurable reductions in epigenetic age.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also discovered that newer biological age clocks performed better than older versions. Another vital finding was that people living with diseases generally experienced larger changes in their aging biomarkers than healthy participants.

Could DNA Blood Tests Transform Anti-Aging Research?

According to Sehgal, the next priority is to test these findings in larger, more diverse populations. This would help researchers determine how consistently different treatments influence biological aging across people with different health conditions and backgrounds.

The improved blood tests could also dramatically shorten the time needed to evaluate potential anti-aging therapies.

"If these new biomarkers are eventually validated to predict long-term health, scientists will be able to evaluate anti-aging therapies much faster," he added. "Instead of waiting decades for evidence from clinical trials, we'll be able to see which interventions are effective and in which people in a few years or even months.".

That possibility could represent a major advance for aging research. Instead of relying entirely on clinical studies that follow participants for decades, scientists might eventually use validated biological age measurements to identify promising treatments much earlier.

However, senior author Higgins-Chen stressed that scientists must be careful about interpreting what changes in aging biomarkers actually mean.

"We have developed a rigorous, systematic approach to evaluating and comparing how biomarkers change across a wide variety of interventions, and that is a critical step in the right direction," he mentioned. "However, the true meaning of that change must be fully understood.".

Vital Questions About Slowing Aging Remain.

Although the results are promising, several major questions remain unanswered.

Industry observers note that for example, researchers still need to establish whether changes in biological age are directly caused by a treatment or influenced by other factors that were not accounted for. They also need to understand how quickly those changes occur, whether they persist after treatment ends, and which biological processes produce them.

Most importantly, scientists have not yet established whether lowering epigenetic age leads to meaningful improvements in long-term health.

"And most importantly - what does the change mean for our long-term risk of age-related disease and functional decline?" Higgins-Chen said.

Further investigations into these questions are underway, with additional studies led by Borrus, Armstrong, and Grace Zou.

The Higgins-Chen laboratory is also affiliated with Yale's Department of Pathology, the Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Program, and the Y-Age Yale Center for Research on Aging.

What Appears to Work Against Biological Aging?

Based on the improved DNA-based blood tests, the Yale researchers identified two particularly promising approaches for reducing biological age markers:.

The analysis also identified benefits from certain anti-TNF medications, while the tested over-the-counter supplements and some medical procedures showed little measurable effect.

Recent findings suggest that these results provide a clearer picture of which interventions may influence biological aging. However, more research is needed to confirm the findings and determine whether reductions in biological age markers ultimately translate into fewer age-related diseases, better health, or longer lives.

#707. Industry News: I finally got a USB-C charging e-bike, and it costs 75% less than Rivian’s bike

📅 14 Nov 2026

Industry News: I finally got a USB-C charging e-bike, and it costs 75% less than Rivian’s bike

Tanggal: 14 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://electrek.co/2026/11/14/i-finally-got-a-usb-c-charging-e-bike-and-it-costs-75-less-than-rivians-bike/

I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging. We’ve already standardized much of our lives around the convenient little connector, from phones and laptops to tablets and countless other gadgets. But for some reason, electric bikes have largely missed the memo. Now, though, I’m finally riding an e-bike that charges with USB-C, and the best part is that it doesn’t cost an arm and a leg.

Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has quickly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a significant difference.

When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.

Sources indicate that USB-C charging on electric bikes isn’t entirely latest, but it’s surprisingly rare. Ampler was one of the first companies to introduce it barely a year ago, though its bikes are sadly no longer in production after the company’s bankruptcy. More recently, Rivian’s ALSO electric bike arrived with USB-C charging, but that bike costs around $4,500 – at least if you want the model that’s slowly starting to ship.

Recent findings suggest that the ENGWE Zip, on the other hand, costs roughly a quarter as much as its only USB-charging competition. At €999, it’s priced at a relatively affordable US$1,100. That’s a quarter of the cost of the only other USB-C charging e-bike on the market.

Sources indicate that of course, it’s not nearly as technologically advanced as Rivian’s ALSO e-bike. But hey, it’s at least shipping.

And while the Zip is a fun little 16″ wheel folding electric bike in its own right, with a compact design that makes it easy to store and transport, it’s the charging setup that has me particularly excited.

Instead of keeping track of yet another proprietary charging brick, I can simply grab the USB-C charger from my laptop and plug it into the bike. There’s one in my living room by the couch. There’s one by my bed. There’s one in all of my friends’ places. There’s a USB-C charger everywhere.

It has been revealed that if I’m traveling around, that means one less charger to pack. If I’m visiting someone, there’s a decent chance they already have a compatible charger sitting around.

Heck, I can even use a basic USB-C phone charger in a pinch. Sure, charging a relatively large e-bike battery at 20W isn’t going to be particularly quick, but the fact that I can do it at all is incredibly convenient.

Plus, the bike has one more trick. The battery also outputs USB-C, so I can charge my laptop or other devices from it as well. I can even charge two devices simultaneously, thanks to the dual USB-C ports.

The battery is housed in a roll-top bag that is locked into the headset of the bike but can be promptly unlocked for charging off the bike. And since it’s a keyed lock, no one can steal the battery even when the bag is left on the bike.

I typically charge the battery still mounted on the bike, though occasionally when I want to use a friend’s USB-C charger, I’ll just pop the bag off and bring it right up to wherever the closest USB-C charger is located.

Recent findings suggest that it may not be the fastest charge, but it’s pretty darn convenient. And with a 360Wh battery, a powerful 100W laptop charger will still get it pretty much full in 4 hours, or for a more typical 50% recharge, roughly two hours.

And that’s really the beauty of USB-C charging. It’s not necessarily about charging faster. It’s about having options. It’s about not being stuck if the very specific charger that only works on your e-bike doesn’t happen to be around exactly where you are.

Of course, there’s a technical reason we haven’t seen USB-C charging spread across the e-bike industry quite as swiftly as it has with smaller electronics. Most e-bike batteries operate at 36V or 48V nominal, meaning their charging voltages are higher than the 20V typically supplied by common USB-C laptop chargers. That requires additional voltage conversion and charging circuitry inside the bike or battery.

In a recent development, but clearly, it can be done. And if ENGWE can offer it on a €999 electric bike, there’s a pretty compelling argument that more manufacturers should be taking a serious look at the technology. In this case, it’s all housed inside the battery, meaning it could be directly incorporated into any e-bike whose manufacturer is brave enough to spec it.

Sources indicate that I’m not suggesting that every e-bike needs to abandon its dedicated charger tomorrow. For larger batteries, high-powered chargers still make plenty of sense, especially when you want to get back on the road quickly.

But having USB-C as an additional charging option? That’s something I’d love to see become standard.

It has been revealed that for years, we’ve seen how electric bikes are becoming more convenient, more practical, and better integrated into our everyday lives. Yet when it comes to charging, we’re still carrying around a collection of more or less proprietary chargers.

In a recent development, now I’m riding a barely $1k electric bike that can charge from the same power brick as my laptop. And frankly, I think it’s about time the rest of the e-bike industry caught up!

#709. Industry News: A latest fiber supplement could help millions suffering from irritable bowel syndrome

📅 14 Nov 2026

Industry News: A latest fiber supplement could help millions suffering from irritable bowel syndrome

Tanggal: 14 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261112230450.htm

Sources indicate that A specially designed fiber supplement may offer a promising upcoming way to improve gut health for millions of people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Researchers at Edith Cowan University (ECU) have developed and tested a fiber combination that supports beneficial gut bacteria without making common digestive symptoms worse.

The research team at ECU's Nutrition and Health Innovation Research Institute (NHIRI) found that the supplement, called ur gut®, improved gut health in people with IBS without increasing abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, or constipation.

IBS affects people around the world, including nearly 11 percent of Australians. Although its exact cause remains unclear, stress, infections, and certain medications may contribute to the condition. Symptoms can also become worse because of particular foods, inadequate sleep, psychological stress, hormonal changes, and lifestyle factors.

Why Common IBS Diets Can Affect Gut Health.

People with IBS are frequently advised to follow a low-FODMAP diet, which limits certain carbohydrates that are easily fermented by gut bacteria. Although this approach can help control uncomfortable symptoms, restricting these foods may also have unintended consequences for the gut microbiome.

Industry observers note that "For years we've known that a diet low in Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monesaccharides and Polyols (FODMAPs) can relieve symptoms, but they can also reduce beneficial gut bacteria and negatively impact fiber intake over time," lead author Dr. Tina Yan remarked.

"We wanted to find a way to build better gut health while following a low-FODMAP diet.".

The upcoming findings suggest that a carefully formulated fiber supplement could help address this problem, allowing people with IBS to support a healthier gut microbiome while continuing to manage their symptoms through dietary changes.

The researchers attribute the supplement's promising effects to its combination of two ingredients: resistant starch and psyllium husk.

It has been revealed that psyllium appears to slow the breakdown of resistant starch by gut bacteria, allowing more of it to reach deeper sections of the colon before fermentation occurs. This process may increase the production of beneficial compounds that support intestinal health.

Ordinarily, fermentable fiber can be challenging for people with IBS because bacterial fermentation can produce excess gas and increase digestive discomfort. The new formulation appears to offer a way to obtain the benefits of fermentation without aggravating these symptoms.

According to recent reports, "Traditionally, fermentable fibers can be difficult for people with IBS because they can increase gas production and discomfort," Dr. Yan remarked.

"What's exciting about this study is that participants maintained stable symptoms while showing meaningful improvements in their gut microbiota as well as in their gut-related anxiety.".

Significant Changes in Gut Bacteria and Anxiety.

The researchers observed substantial shifts in the composition of participants' gut bacteria during the intervention. These changes were particularly notable because they occurred over a relatively short period.

"Changes of this magnitude are rarely seen with such a short intervention," ur gut® co-creator Professor Amanda Devine stated.

In a recent development, "The study demonstrated that our targeted dietary fiber blend positively reshaped the gut microbiome in people with IBS following a low-FODMAP diet, supporting beneficial bacteria linked to gut and mental health. This was great to see.".

It has been revealed that alongside improvements in gut bacteria, participants also experienced reductions in gut-related anxiety. These findings suggest that the supplement's potential benefits may extend beyond changes in the digestive system, although further research will be needed to establish its broader effects.

A Fresh Approach to Managing Irritable Bowel Syndrome.

The researchers believe their findings could help shift IBS care toward improving the underlying health of the gut rather than focusing exclusively on avoiding foods that cause discomfort.

"For many people with IBS, success has traditionally meant simply avoiding certain foods," ur gut® co-creator Associate Professor Claus Christophersen mentioned.

"Our findings suggest we may also be able to actively rebuild gut health and the microbiome while not making IBS symptoms worse. That's an vital step forward.".

By demonstrating that beneficial gut bacteria can be supported without increasing IBS symptoms, the study points toward newly introduced dietary strategies that could complement existing treatments.

Recent findings suggest that the ur gut® supplement is already available for purchase. The research team has also created a cookbook featuring recipes designed to help people incorporate the supplement into a healthy diet.

The study, "Dietary fibre blend improves gut health in patients with irritable bowel syndrome following a low FODMAP diet: a randomised, double-blind control trial," was published online in the European Journal of Nutrition.

According to recent reports, heads up stargazers! Mars meets Jupiter for a spectacular rendezvous in the heart of the constellation Leo on the night of Nov. 15-16, and they won't be this close again until July 2029.

Jupiter and Mars will appear a little over 1 degree from each other as they rise over the eastern horizon around midnight for viewers in the U.S., as the blue-white light of the main-sequence star Regulus glows below, according to In-The-Sky.

It's all a trick of perspective, but spectacular nonetheless. In reality Mars and Jupiter are separated by a gulf of over 368 million miles (592 million kilometers), while the light from Regulus has travelled for some 79 light-years before reaching Earth.

The spectacular display occurs just once every 2-2.5 years, when Mars catches up to Jupiter as it plies its more distant orbit, making the pair appear side by side from our Earthly vantage point — an event known to astronomers as an appulse.

It has been revealed that both Mars and Jupiter are "superior planets" whose orbits exist beyond that of Earth. As a result their disks always appear full to us through the eyepiece of a telescope, unlike the inner planets Mercury and Venus, which exhibit moon-like phases as they circle the sun.

A 6-inch telescope can reveal the wildly differing natures of the solar system worlds. Slew your scope to Jupiter to spot the gargantuan cloud bands (and zones) that ring the gas giant, formed from masses of ammonia and water that travel in different directions through Jupiter's hydrogen and helium atmosphere, driven by powerful jet streams.

Mars, meanwhile, appears as a reddish, ochre disk complete with dark surface features, where basaltic rock has been scoured clean of the iron-rich dust that covers much of its surface, according to NASA.

‘I Picked Up Weights for the First Time in My Mid-50s. I Was Powerlifting by My 70s—Here’s How’

“Getting stronger takes patience, consistency, and a willingness to step outside my comfort zone, but the reward is so worth it.”.

Industry observers note that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

If I’ve learned anything over the past few years, it’s to just say yes. Saying the word was simple, but ended up changing my relationship with fitness—and transforming my whole life.

I’ve always loved being physically active and moving my body; I ran track and field in high school, played field hockey in both high school and college, and enjoyed horseback riding as a young adult. But shortly after graduating, I had my first of seven children at 23. From that point on, I went straight into parenting mode: My family became my priority, and with so much to juggle, exercise took a back seat for the next few decades.

Recent findings suggest that but at 55, I wanted to feel strong in my body again. My kids were grown and I had more free time, so I signed up for a gym membership. I even started working with a personal trainer to make sure I was doing the right moves safely. Over the next 15 years, I exercised with several trainers, lifting light weights once or twice a week with dumbbells and weight machines. I enjoyed the workouts and saw improvements to my overall fitness, but I wasn’t particularly passionate about going to the gym, so I wasn’t always consistent and never set any real goals.

According to recent reports, then, at 70, everything changed. My trainer who I had come to enjoy working with and trust moved away, and without that connection, I stopped going to the gym. But after about a year away, the fitness manager at my gym, Nate Fleming, reached out to me, and I began working with him twice a week.

Industry observers note that he immediately changed up my programming and introduced me to the idea of progressive overload. I learned that gradually increasing the weight I lifted each week could help me build muscle, get stronger, and see real results. He also added new movements to my routine, like farmer’s carries, deadlifts, and squat variations. Deadlifts, in particular, became one of my favorite exercises—I loved that the move required so much technique. There was something so satisfying about picking up a heavy weight and realizing I could lift more than I thought.

In a recent development, nearly overnight, my attitude toward fitness changed: I enjoyed being challenged and discovering how much stronger I could become when I pushed myself. Over the next year, I began to see visible muscle definition in my arms and legs and felt more energized throughout the day. More importantly, though, my confidence skyrocketed because I had developed a greater trust in my own abilities.

I had grown to love lifting heavy, and wanted to step outside my comfort zone and discover what I could accomplish in my 70s. I casually asked Nate if there were deadlifting competitions for older women, and he said there were. So, I took a leap of faith and started a seven-month training process for a powerlifting competition (which took place this past March). I upped my training to three days a week, continuing to progressively increase the weights, and worked on refining my technique to move more efficiently.

The day of the competition was one of the best days of my life. I decided to compete in all three lifts: I squatted 132 pounds, bench-pressed 71.5 pounds, and deadlifted 242 pounds, setting records in all three lifts for my age and weight category in Nova Scotia, Canada, where I live. I was so proud of what I’d accomplished and felt incredibly empowered by what my body could do at 71. My kids and grandkids were also there to cheer me on, which made the day even more special. Sharing that moment with my family and showing them what was possible at my age meant so much to me. I walked away feeling stronger, more confident, and excited to do it again.

Recent findings suggest that my next powerlifting competition is this month, and I still lift with Nate three days a week. My training is structured in four-week blocks, and the weight, sets, and reps change each week. For instance, in week one, I might do 3 sets of 5 reps at a moderate weight. Then, I gradually increase the load in weeks two and three while lowering the reps as I get closer to my heaviest lifts. Week four is a deload week, so I reduce the weight and give my body a chance to recover before lifting heavier again.

Each workout starts with the main lift (deadlift, squat, or bench press) because that’s when I have the most energy. Then, I move on to three or four accessory exercises, where I use lighter weights to strengthen supporting muscles, address weaknesses, and improve my performance in the main lifts. For example, on deadlift day, I might incorporate exercises like lunges, hamstring curls, and bent-over rows to strengthen my glutes, hamstrings, and back.

I’m incredibly proud of my progress over the last six months. I have a lingering shoulder injury, so right now, my bench press has stayed about the same at 71.5 pounds. But I can squat 160 pounds and deadlift 265 pounds, which is only five pounds away from the Canadian deadlift record.

Sources indicate that while I train hard, I recover even harder in between sessions. I get seven to eight hours of sleep each night and am mindful about nutrition, eating lots of protein, since it’s important for building and maintaining muscle. I aim for around 120 grams a day, with eggs, chicken, and fish as some of my go-to sources. Additionally, during rest days, I focus on stretching and hip and shoulder mobility to improve my range of motion. I don’t count my steps, but I try to walk as much as I can throughout the day to keep my body moving and maintain cardiovascular health.

I love Feetures socks for their snug arch support and gentle compression that keeps them comfortably in place during workouts.

Clif Builders are my favorite post-workout snack since they taste great and pack 20 g of protein per bar.

When I first decided to work with a personal trainer in my 50s, I wanted guidance, accountability, and the confidence that I was exercising safely and effectively—and I got that. My first few trainers helped me build a foundation by teaching me proper form and the fundamental movements that I still rely on today.

Recent findings suggest that but working with Nate completely changed my relationship with lifting: He knows how to motivate me, pushing me without going beyond my abilities. When I attempt a fresh personal record, his belief in me helps me believe in myself, too. Now, I know what I’m capable of and how to challenge myself while lifting safely. The gym has become so much more than a place to work out—it’s where I keep discovering what I can do.

In a recent development, I’ve learned that getting stronger isn’t just about how hard I work in the gym—it’s also about how well I recover between workouts through getting plenty of sleep, mobility work, stretching, and walking. When I don’t make time for recovery activities or I don’t fuel properly, it makes a difference; I feel more fatigued, have less energy during workouts, and struggle to perform at the same level.

For me, progress doesn’t mean pushing myself to the limit every day. It means finding the right balance between challenging my body and giving it the rest and support it needs to keep getting stronger.

In a recent development, if you’d told me a few years ago that I’d be powerlifting in my 70s and chasing a deadlift record, I never would have believed you. Before I started training with Nate, I had never really set significant fitness goals or thought about pushing my limits. But that began to change when I realized how much stronger I could become with the right coaching and encouragement. I was inspired to set goals that challenged me in fresh ways I never thought possible, and I’ve learned that it’s never too late to surprise myself and try something new. Having a goal to work toward keeps me motivated, and I love seeing how far I can push myself when I have the right support and initiative in place.

Of course, getting stronger takes patience, consistency, and a willingness to step outside my comfort zone, but the reward is so worth it. I hope my journey encourages other women, especially those in their 60s and 70s, to keep challenging themselves and try new things. They might discover a passion they never knew they had, just as I did.

#713. A giant icy world hiding beyond Pluto could be our sixth dwarf planet

📅 14 Nov 2026

A giant icy world hiding beyond Pluto could be our sixth dwarf planet

Tanggal: 14 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261112230447.htm

An enormous icy world discovered beyond Pluto could soon become the sixth officially recognized dwarf planet in our solar system.

The object, temporarily named 2026 ED138, was identified by an astronomer analyzing observations from the Simonyi Survey Telescope at the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Early estimates suggest it ranks among the largest dwarf planet candidates ever found beyond Neptune. If its status is confirmed, it would join the five dwarf planets presently recognized by the International Astronomical Union: Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake.

In a recent development, the discovery was confirmed at a press conference featuring Matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, and Mario Jurić, a University of Washington astronomy professor who leads Rubin's solar system team. Holman made the initial discovery, while Jurić helped gather the additional evidence needed to verify it.

Industry observers note that "If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds," Holman noted. "Rubin will image the whole southern sky again and again for 10 years, so any others hiding in the places earlier surveys skipped are now within reach.".

Recent findings suggest that "Finding an object this big, roughly 1,000 kilometers across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation," Jurić noted. "It's the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope.".

How Astronomers Discovered the Hidden World.

In a recent development, the breakthrough occurred on the evening of October 13, when Holman examined observations gathered by Rubin earlier in 2026. He was using specialized software developed with his colleague Kevin Napier to search for previously unidentified objects moving through the solar system.

It has been revealed that the program compares billions of telescope detections, looking for individual points of light that appear in multiple observations and move in ways that suggest they belong to the same object. When the software identified ED138, Holman quickly realized that its apparent brightness and enormous distance pointed to something unusually large.

"My first reaction was one of excited disbelief," Holman stated. "Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong.".

Sources indicate that to check the finding, Jurić examined Rubin's stored observations and located 20 additional detections of ED138, including some captured as early as March 2026. The researchers then searched historical records from other astronomical surveys and identified images of the object dating back to 2016.

Together, these observations allowed the team to reconstruct more than a decade of the distant world's orbital motion, strengthening the evidence that the discovery was genuine.

Could This Be Our Solar System's Sixth Dwarf Planet?

Sources indicate that ED138 currently lies approximately 46 astronomical units (au) from the Sun. One astronomical unit represents the average distance separating Earth and the Sun. By comparison, Pluto's average orbital distance is about 40 au.

Sources indicate that because ED138 travels beyond Neptune, astronomers classify it as a trans-Neptunian object (TNO). These distant bodies are valuable to scientists because their physical properties and orbital paths preserve clues about the solar system's distant past.

By examining their sizes, compositions, and movements, researchers can better understand how the solar system developed, how its giant planets shifted positions, and how smaller bodies were redistributed during that process.

However, being a trans-Neptunian object does not automatically make ED138 a dwarf planet. An essential requirement is that the object's gravity must be strong enough to shape it into a nearly round body.

Using measurements of ED138's brightness and distance, along with estimates of how much sunlight its surface reflects, astronomers calculate that it could measure anywhere from 600 to 1,500 kilometers across.

Sources indicate that an icy object within that size range would generally be expected to have enough gravity to become round. Nevertheless, scientists will need more observations to establish ED138's actual dimensions and determine whether it qualifies as a dwarf planet.

Why Such a Massive World Remained Undiscovered.

One of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is how an object this large managed to escape detection for so long.

It has been revealed that ED138 occupies a region of the sky near the plane of the Milky Way, where millions of stars create an exceptionally crowded background. Against that dense field of light, the distant object's faint movement was difficult for earlier telescopes and surveys to distinguish.

According to recent reports, rubin Observatory has an notable advantage. Its ability to repeatedly observe the Southern Hemisphere sky, combined with advanced computer algorithms, makes it possible to search enormous quantities of astronomical data for subtle changes in the positions of objects.

By examining millions or even billions of individual light detections, these systems can recognize the movement of small solar system bodies that might otherwise disappear into the surrounding stars. This capability was essential to finding ED138 in such a challenging part of the sky.

Rubin Observatory Could Reveal More Hidden Worlds.

The newly identified object adds to a growing collection of solar system discoveries made by Rubin Observatory as it began gathering observations ahead of its ambitious Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), which officially started in June 2026.

Industry observers note that even before the survey began, the observatory was producing remarkable results. In April, Rubin's solar system researchers reported observations of more than 11,000 previously unknown asteroids, including approximately 380 fresh trans-Neptunian objects.

The team described that enormous collection of discoveries as "the tip of the iceberg," anticipating that the full survey would uncover many more objects. The identification of ED138 offers an early indication of just how significant those future findings could be.

In a recent development, rubin's combination of extensive sky coverage, sensitivity, and rapid observations is also changing how astronomers investigate latest discoveries. Once an object has been identified, researchers can search older telescope images to find instances when it was photographed but went unrecognized.

According to recent reports, "Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth, and precision," Jurić stated. "And the discovery is just the beginning: Once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look. This ability to both discover and 'precover' objects is transforming how quickly and accurately we can determine their orbits and understand the distant solar system.".

As Rubin continues surveying the southern sky over the next decade, astronomers expect its observations to uncover additional objects that previous searches missed, potentially revealing more large, icy worlds in the outer solar system.

Anyone interested in exploring ED138 can view its location and orbit using Orbitviewer, an interactive web-based application that displays the solar system in three dimensions and allows consumers to explore its structure in real time.

In a recent development, operations of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory are funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Science.

#714. Hailey Bieber States She's Been Diagnosed With PMDD: What Are the Signs, Symptoms?

Hailey Bieber States She's Been Diagnosed With PMDD: What Are the Signs, Symptoms?

Tanggal: 14 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.healthline.com/health-news/hailey-bieber-diagnosed-with-pmdd-signs-symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Hailey Bieber is sharing her experience with premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), a condition she states has fueled her growing interest in women’s health research.

The Rhode Beauty founder recently confirmed a $5 million, three-year partnership with the Foundation for Women’s Health in an interview with Women’s Wear Daily (WWD).

“As a woman, I feel frustrated by the lack of research, the lack of awareness, the lack of certain conversation around it,” Bieber told WWD.

Motherhood has also shaped her perspective. Bieber welcomed her son, Jack Blues, with her husband, Justin Bieber, in 2024, describing the experience as a “really intense and special journey.”.

She also shared that she “struggled” with PMDD after giving birth, noting that there’s “not a lot of conversation or research around it.”.

“When we can identify with each other and have conversations relating to each other and talking about the things we’re dealing with and struggling with, I do think it makes it feel like less of a lonely journey,” Bieber said.

PMDD is a complexcondition that causes severe physical and psychological symptoms that typically occur in the days or weeks leading up to menstruation.

“What distinguishes PMDD from the more common PMS (premenstrual syndrome) is the severity of the symptoms and how significantly they can interfere with daily functioning,” Sari Eitches, MD, dual board certified physician and medical advisor to Terra Mare, told Healthline.

“Another defining feature is the timing: symptoms typically worsen in the week or two before a period, resolve within a few days after menstruation begins, and are minimal or absent during the rest of the cycle,” she noted.

Eitches also noted that PMDD is a chronic condition that can affect women at any stage of their reproductive lives, from adolescence through perimenopause, as long as they are having menstrual cycles.

“It is caused by a sensitivity to cyclic hormonal and neurotransmitter fluctuations, so [it] can occur in anyone with a menstrual cycle, though stages of hormonal fluctuation- including postpartum, weaning breastfeeding, and perimenopause- can be a trigger,” she added.

According to research published in 2024, approximately 1.6% of women and girls meet the strict diagnostic criteria for PMDD, equivalent to an estimated 31 million people worldwide.

A higher percentage of 3.2% have a provisional diagnosis, meaning a healthcare professional may believe a person has PMDD, but symptoms have not been measured for a sustained amount of time to meet the criteria for a confirmed diagnosis.

Eitches noted that women with a personal or family history of depression or anxiety may be more prone to developing PMDD, as are women with a family history of PMDD itself.

In a recent development, “PMDD is understood to be caused by a combination of heritable biological sensitivities and environmental triggers. These can include a history of trauma, chronic stress, and other chronic medical conditions,” she noted.

Eitches also said that you should consider seeing a doctor if your symptoms are severe enough that they’re interfering with your ability to go to work or school, maintain your relationships, or participate in your life in the same way that you do during the other weeks of the month.

In a recent development, to diagnose PMDD, a healthcare professional will review your medical history and symptoms and may perform a physical exam. They will typically ask you to track your symptoms over at least two menstrual cycles.

A PMDD diagnosis generally requires at least five symptoms, including at least one mood-related symptom, that occur before menstruation, improve shortly after a period begins, and significantly interfere with daily life.

Treatment options for PMDD include prescription medications and over-the-counter treatments that may help relieve certain symptoms, such as:.

Eitches noted that cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can also help manage symptoms.

Lifestyle changes may also help manage PMDD symptoms, including practicing relaxation techniques, eating a balanced diet, limiting sugary and salty foods, and getting regular physical activity.

Eitches noted that getting enough high quality sleep and resting on a consistent schedule is also notable.

“I also recommend focusing on a whole-foods-based diet, limiting added sugar and caffeine, and avoiding cigarette smoking,” she mentioned.

#715. Who Knew Spirituality Might Prevent Addiction and Relapse?

📅 14 Nov 2026

Who Knew Spirituality Might Prevent Addiction and Relapse?

Tanggal: 14 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/addiction-outlook/202611/who-knew-spirituality-might-prevent-addiction-and-relapse

In a recent development, after years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

In a recent development, self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

I have studied addiction from the laboratory bench to the bedside for more than 50 years. In that time, we’ve learned a great deal about addiction, withdrawal, craving, treatment, and relapse. And we now understand that dopamine, reward, stress, and some brain changes make quitting extremely difficult.

But what is the crux of addiction that makes it so difficult to treat? How do some people stop using while others relapse repeatedly, sometimes fatally?

According to recent reports, alcoholics Anonymous (A.A.) offered an answer long before neuroscientists could look at dopamine in the living brain. Putting a stop to drinking is only the beginning.

Recent findings suggest that when Bill Wilson and Dr. Bob Smith founded Alcoholics Anonymous in 1935, they weren’t thinking about dopamine. They knew addiction and recovery from the patient's perspective. Nearly a century later, neuroscience is catching up. What A.A. called “spirituality” may involve measurable changes in thinking, behavior, social connections, and brain function. A.A. began with clinical observation and lived experience. Modern neuroscience is helping explain why recovery works.

Smith famously summarized A.A.’s core work as simply "love and service." Helping newcomers gives recovering individuals a sense of meaning, boosts self-efficacy (confidence in staying sober), and breaks the cycle of obsessive self-focus.

People might struggle to remember who and what they were before they developed a substance use disorder (SUD). Treatment is tough; it takes time, and people need persistence and resilience. With continued treatment, good things may then happen—relationships, accountability, purpose, and hope.

Recent findings suggest that true, A.A. has spiritual roots, but it’s not a religion. A.A. members are encouraged to find a power greater than themselves. That may be God, or helping others, or something else. Spirituality has always been part of the A.A. founders' core message and approach. Now science is catching up. But what exactly is spirituality doing?

In a recent 2026 JAMA Psychiatry meta-analysis, Howard Koh and colleagues examined 55 longitudinal studies involving 540,712 people. Religious or spiritual involvement was associated with a 13% lower relative risk of harmful alcohol or other substance use. More-than-weekly religious-service attendance was associated with an 18% lower risk.

It has been revealed that association is not causation, but these are still impressive numbers. People involved in religious communities may also have more supportive families, different friends, greater supervision, and social expectations discouraging drug use, which may influence the numbers.

Sources indicate that there’s another important thing to remember about this study. About 87% of the study’s extracted effects concerned prevention. Preventing addiction and treating established addiction aren’t the same thing.

Recent findings suggest that another study added crucial information. Paul McClure and Lindsay Wilkinson examined 1,711 adults in the Midlife Development in the United States study. People who attended substance-use recovery groups were 2-3 times more likely to identify as spiritual but not religious. More frequent participation was particularly associated with this identity.

Recent findings suggest that anyone who has treated SUDs has seen patients who seemed absolutely hopeless. But people surprise themselves and us all the time. They change in ways that cannot be explained by a negative urine drug screen.

In a recent development, addiction changes priorities. Family, work, relationships, and ordinary pleasures lose their appeal. Behavior and motivation shift from everyday rewards to drugs and drug-related cues.

Drug consumers remember that drugs produced pleasure. But that becomes a memory. Over time, continued use becomes increasingly prompted by the need to avoid withdrawal, dysphoria, and distress. The next drink, dose, or high takes priority.

Many patients entering treatment are depressed, anxious, and unable to experience pleasure. Some have independent psychiatric disorders. Others have symptoms produced or amplified by chronic substance use and withdrawal.

In a recent development, detox or cold turkey stopping the drug does not immediately restore normal brain or reward function. This is one reason early recovery is so difficult. The drug is gone, but pleasure, motivation, and hope may not have returned.

We don’t have evidence that prayer restores dopamine neurons or reverses addiction-related neuroadaptations. Those claims would go well beyond the science. But consider what happens in a recovery community. A meeting provides structure. A sponsor provides accountability. A recovering person helps someone newly sober, consolidating their own sobriety. Friendships develop. People resume positive activities they had ended with addiction.

In a recent development, people with SUDs find it hard to believe that helping another person can become more rewarding than getting high. But when they change, helping others can become a reason for living. These changes may be essential to sustained recovery.

In a recent development, the brain learns from experience. Recovery requires fresh experiences, new habits, and new rewards.

In a recent development, A.A. has been helping people recover since 1935 through personal testimony rather than rigorous clinical research. Then a 2020 Cochrane review of 27 studies found that manualized A.A. and Twelve-Step Facilitation often produced better continuous abstinence outcomes in alcohol use disorder than other established treatments.

Recent findings suggest that john Kelly is the expert on how A.A. works. Kelly notes that when social networks change for the better, coping improves. Abstinence becomes more acceptable, and recovery becomes part of a person’s identity. A.A. does not work because someone is told to believe in God (which A.A. does not do). It may work because people change their behavior, their friends, their expectations, and their lives.

Sources indicate that research is finally asking the big questions. Do religious or spiritual involvement reduce the risk of developing harmful substance use? The 2026 meta-analysis suggests it may.

Can A.A. improve recovery after alcohol use disorder has developed? Randomized trials and systematic reviews support that conclusion.

While these are different questions, we know that spirituality is relevant to SUD risk and is also very helpful in SUD treatment.

In a recent development, SUDs develop quickly because of secrecy, stigma, fear, and deep shame. Admitting powerlessness and ceding control to a "Higher Power"—whether defined as God, nature, or the collective wisdom of the group—can help by relieving the crushing burden of trying to control everything alone.

It has been revealed that it is up to the individual to figure out. But some patients derive strength from organized religion. Others reject religion but find purpose in service, meditation, nature, family, or secular recovery groups.

In a recent development, what matters most isn’t whether someone attends church. It is whether they have relationships, purpose, and support that help them stay well.

Ask whether religion or spirituality matters to this patient. Has it helped during difficult times? Does the patient want spirituality included in treatment?

According to recent reports, spirituality is not a replacement for medicine, and a sponsor is not a substitute for a physician. Patients with opioid use disorder need medications like buprenorphine or methadone. Severe alcohol withdrawal requires medical detox and naltrexone. Depression, psychosis, and trauma require appropriate assessment and treatment.

Addiction hijacks the brain’s dopamine and pleasure pathways. Spiritual practices like prayer, meditation, and intense fellowship stimulate similar reward and emotional-regulation centers in the brain, affording a healthy psychological substitute. But recovery programs also change how people live, whom they trust, what they value, and what they look forward to.

Stopping drug use is essential, but so is building a life worth staying sober for.

#716. Tesla Cybercab orders open at $29,990 + $299/mo, only in Robotaxi zones

📅 14 Nov 2026

Tesla Cybercab orders open at $29,990 + $299/mo, only in Robotaxi zones

Tanggal: 14 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://electrek.co/2026/11/13/tesla-cybercab-personal-use-orders-299-subscription-geofence/

Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”.

And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.

Tesla’s official Robotaxi account unveiled the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.

In a recent development, the order page lists the Cybercab at $29,990 before taxes, with an estimated delivery of December 2026 in Austin, Texas. You need to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit to order.

Industry observers note that the subscription isn’t optional. It’s pre-checked on the order page at $299 per month, with one month included, and the fine print notes “Subscription and regular vehicle maintenance required to operate.”.

Recent findings suggest that the email is even more direct. Its asterisk reads: “Only available in supported service areas. Subscription required for operation.”.

Industry observers note that the rest is what we already knew. Two seats, a 21-inch center touchscreen, 20.1 cubic feet of cargo space, and no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla calls it “fully autonomous” and says you’ll “manage your ride in the app.”.

Musk had promised a Cybercab “below $30,000” when he unveiled it in 2024. He technically hit it. He just didn’t mention the $3,588 a year it takes to use it. Over five years, that’s about $47,600 for a two-seater, before insurance, maintenance, taxes, and charging.

Tesla runs its Robotaxi service in eight cities: Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, and San Antonio in Texas, and Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. That’s where a Cybercab can operate. Everywhere else, it’s a $30,000 sculpture in your driveway.

And those service areas aren’t what Tesla indicates they are. Independent tracker Koby Pierce tested thousands of addresses in the Robotaxi app and found that the areas where Tesla actually accepts pickups and drop-offs are only 59% to 78% of the advertised geofences in the six cities he checked. In Austin, the very city where Tesla is delivering these cars, it’s about 59%.

Recent findings suggest that railroad crossings are a big reason why. In Houston, the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app quoting about 40 minutes to go two blocks downtown because the vehicle appeared to route around rail crossings. Tesla also lists San Antonio’s airport inside its polygon but doesn’t serve it.

Then there’s the regulatory cloud. NHTSA has ordered Tesla to prove under oath that a car with no brake pedal meets federal safety standards that require one. Tesla answered on October 30 and asked that the entire response be kept confidential. NHTSA hasn’t ruled. Tesla is now selling the car to consumers anyway.

I think this is going to be a total mess. It looks like Tesla is only doing this by invitation and delivering it in Austin to prove they can deliver an “unsupervised” vehicle in 2026.

Tesla is going to sell these to fans who are excited about owning a self-driving car, and many of them will find out the limitations aren’t worth $299 a month on top of a $30,000 car.

Sure, if your monthly Uber bill is well over $300 and you live and work deep inside the geofence, maybe the math works on paper. Until you realize you have to park it somewhere once you get to your destination. Or that it can’t take you to a friend’s place two neighborhoods over. Or that a 15-minute drive turns into an hour because the car won’t cross a train track. With an Uber or a Waymo, that’s someone else’s problem. With a Cybercab, you’re paying for the privilege.

No point trying to calculate what it will cost over X years. Tesla can change that monthly fee at will anyway (and shall be expected to, considering their overall pricing history).

According to recent reports, and here’s the part that makes no sense to me. The Cybercab runs on the same AI4 computer as the current Model Y. Tesla already runs unsupervised Model Y Robotaxis in these same geofences. So why can’t the Model Y owners who already paid for “Full Self-Driving” get unsupervised operation in those same zones? Wouldn’t be even easier to turn that on these vehicles which have accumulated much more data? Tesla keeps pushing that to “next year,” presently around Q2 2027, while asking people to buy a upcoming two-seater that can do nothing else.

Industry observers note that if the tech works unsupervised in Austin, turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin. If it doesn’t, why should anyone pay $47,000 over five years for a car that only works where Tesla states it does?

Like with every other Tesla product lately, the delivered version is going to be a lot more disappointing than the one that was sold on stage.

#719. This Common Drug Was Just Linked to a 24% Lower Risk of Dementia

📅 14 Nov 2026

This Common Drug Was Just Linked to a 24% Lower Risk of Dementia

Tanggal: 14 Nov 2026 | Sumber: https://www.womenshealthmag.com/health/a74425105/osteoporosis-drug-dementia-risk/

According to recent reports, for all of the havoc dementia causes to a person's life, scientists are still trying to figure out exactly how to prevent it. While keeping your brain and body active and following a healthy diet seems to help, there doesn't seem to be a pill you can pop to lower your risk of developing the devastating disease. But fresh research suggests that a common osteoporosis drug might be worth investigating further.

According to recent reports, it's a class of medications called nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (or NBPs). While these are typically used to strengthen bones in people with osteoporosis, NBPs could have the added benefit of supporting brain health as you age, too.

It's important to stress this now: The researchers found a link between people who used NBPs and a lower risk of dementia, but they didn't prove that the medications themselves actually dropped the risk. Still, doctors say there could be something to this. "The association is intriguing," indicates Anna Hohler, MD, director of neurology for Northwell Health's Westchester Region, and chair of neurology at Phelps Hospital and Northern Westchester Hospital.

Here's what experts want you to take away from the findings.

Meet the experts: Ching-Lung Cheung, PhD, study co-author and associate professor in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at the University of Hong Kong; Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John's Health Center in Santa Monica, California; and Anna Hohler, MD, director of neurology for Northwell Health's Westchester Region, and chair of neurology at Phelps Hospital and Northern Westchester Hospital.

The study, which was published in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia, analyzed the electronic medical records of more than 120,000 patients aged 60 and older in Hong Kong. All of the participants had osteoporosis or fractures due to fragility (meaning, their bones had weakened).

Researchers discovered that people who took NBPs had a 16 percent lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease and related dementias compared to those who didn't take medication for osteoporosis. But when they compared those who used NBPs to those taking other types of osteoporosis medications, the dementia risk was 24 percent lower.

The link seemed to be especially strong in women and patients who had hip fractures.

It has been revealed that the researchers were inspired to look into NBPs and Alzheimer’s because the drug had been shown to improve cognitive function in previous animal models of neurotoxicity and Alzheimer’s disease, says Ching-Lung Cheung, PhD, study co-author and associate professor in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at the University of Hong Kong. “These findings led us to investigate whether their use might also be associated with a lower risk of dementia in humans.".

While the study didn't prove that NBPs were responsible for the lowered risk, doctors have a few theories on what could be driving this.

For one, it’s possible that the link is more indirect, according to Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John's Health Center in Santa Monica, California. NBPs improve bone density over time, which allows people to be more active, Dr. Segil says. "Broken bones do not cause dementia but do decrease activity," he says. (Being sedentary is a risk factor for dementia.).

There may also be something about NBPs themselves that could lower the risk of dementia, though. "Some researchers speculate that these medications could influence inflammation, immune pathways, or other biological processes involved in neurodegeneration," Dr. Hoehler says. But, she points out, more research is needed.

According to recent reports, for now, doctors don't initiative to prescribe NBPs in an effort to lower dementia risk. But Dr. Cheung says it should make people feel confident about using this class of medication for bone health. "Given the low uptake of osteoporosis treatment, people with osteoporosis should consider appropriate anti-osteoporosis medication, which may offer an additional benefit for brain health," he says. Even though osteoporosis drugs are commonly available, uptake has been historically low—studies have previously estimated that around seven percent of women with osteoporosis actually take medication for it.

Ultimately, doctors say that a clinical trial is needed to see if NBPs actually lower the risk of dementia. "If future studies confirm these results, they could open an exciting newly introduced avenue for Alzheimer's prevention or treatment," Dr. Hoehler says.

Carina Hsieh, MPH, is the deputy features editor of Women’s Health. She has more than a decade’s worth of experience working in media and has covered everything from beauty, fashion, travel, lifestyle, pets, to health.

She began her career as an intern in the fashion closet at Cosmopolitan where she worked her way up to Senior Sex & Relationships Editor. While covering women’s health there, she discovered her passion for health service journalism and took a break to get her Masters in Public Health. Post-grad school, she worked as a freelance writer and as The Daily Beast’s first Beauty, Health, and Wellness Reporter.

Carina is an alum of the Fashion Institute of Technology and the Yale School of Public Health. She and her French Bulldog, Bao Bao, split their time between Brooklyn and Connecticut. She enjoys reformer Pilates, (slow) running, and smelling the fancy toiletries in boutique fitness class locker rooms.
